hints: Trace the oxygen molecule's exact journey on paper, from alveolar air to inside the red blood cell. How many cell membranes must it cross to get in and out of the alveolar cell, in and out of the capillary cell, and then into the red blood cell?
Add up the two cytoplasms plus the tissue between them, then add $5 \text{ nm}$ for every cell membrane crossed. Remember haemoglobin fills the red cell, so you stop as soon as you enter it.
walkthrough:
**Picture the diffusion route**

Think like the oxygen molecule. You start in the air, then you must go through the alveolar wall cell, across the gap tissue, through the capillary wall cell, then into the red blood cell where haemoglobin is waiting.

Every time you go right through a flat wall cell you cross two membranes, one to enter and one to leave.

**List what must be crossed**

Alveolar wall cell: enter membrane + cytoplasm + leave membrane.
Gap tissue between walls: tissues between alveolar wall and capillary wall.
Capillary wall cell: enter membrane + cytoplasm + leave membrane.
Red blood cell: enter membrane only to reach haemoglobin, because haemoglobin completely fills the cell and the cell touches the capillary wall.

So in total: 2 cytoplasms + 1 gap tissue + 5 membranes.

**Add up the thicknesses**

Cytoplasms and tissue:
$$190 + 90 + 300 = 580 \text{ nm}$$
Membranes:
$$5 \times 5 = 25 \text{ nm}$$
Total shortest distance:
$$580 + 25 = 605 \text{ nm}$$
That matches option C. Well done for counting membranes carefully, this is where most students slip.

options.A: Too small. 595 nm only adds 3 membranes ($580 + 15$), so it misses two membrane crossings on the route.
options.B: Too small. 600 nm only adds 4 membranes ($580 + 20$), so it misses one membrane, often the entry into the red blood cell.
options.C: Correct. 2 alveolar membranes + 2 capillary membranes + 1 red cell entry membrane = 5 membranes ($25 \text{ nm}$) plus $190 + 90 + 300 = 580 \text{ nm}$, giving $605 \text{ nm}$.
options.D: Too large. 610 nm adds 6 membranes ($580 + 30$), which would mean going right through and out of the red blood cell instead of stopping at the haemoglobin inside.
